blocks.text: From between two men who were talking right by the door — the one, with both hands stretched far out before him, was making the motion of counting out money, the other was looking him sharply in the eye — a hand reached for K. It was a small red-cheeked boy. “Come along, come along,” he said. K. let himself be led by him, and it turned out that in the swarming, jostling crowd there was after all a narrow path left free, which possibly divided two parties; this was also suggested by the fact that in the first rows to the right and left K. saw scarcely a face turned towards him, but only the backs of people who directed their speeches and gestures solely to people of their own party. Most of them were dressed in black, in old, long, loosely hanging holiday coats. Only this clothing puzzled K.; otherwise he would have taken the whole thing for a local political meeting.

At the other end of the hall, to which K. was led, there stood on a very low platform, likewise overcrowded, a little table, set crosswise, and behind it, near the edge of the platform, sat a small, fat, wheezing man, who was just then conversing amid great laughter with someone standing behind him — this man had propped his elbow on the back of the chair and crossed his legs. Now and then he flung his arm into the air, as if he were caricaturing someone. The boy who was leading K. had difficulty in delivering his announcement. Twice already, standing on tiptoe, he had tried to convey something, without being noticed by the man up above. Only when one of the people up on the platform drew attention to the boy did the man turn to him and, bending down, listen to his quiet report. Then he drew out his watch and glanced quickly over at K. “You should have appeared 1 hour and 5 minutes ago,” he said. K. wanted to make some reply, but he had no time, for scarcely had the man finished speaking when a general murmuring arose in the right half of the hall. “You should have appeared 1 hour and 5 minutes ago,” the man now repeated in a raised voice, and now he too glanced quickly down into the hall. At once the murmuring grew stronger as well, and, since the man said nothing more, died away only gradually. It was now much quieter in the hall than when K. had come in. Only the people in the gallery did not stop making their remarks. They seemed, so far as one could make anything out up there in the half-darkness, haze and dust, to be worse dressed than those below. Some had brought cushions with them, which they had placed between their heads and the ceiling, so as not to rub themselves sore.

K. had resolved to observe more than to speak, and consequently he dispensed with any defence of his alleged lateness and merely said: “I may have come late, but now I am here.” A burst of applause, again from the right half of the hall, followed. “People easily won over,” thought K., and was troubled only by the silence in the left half of the hall, which lay just behind him and from which only quite scattered clapping had arisen. He considered what he might say in order to win over everyone at once or, should that not be possible, at least for the time being to win over the others as well.

“Yes,” said the man, “but I am no longer obliged to examine you now” — again the murmuring, but this time based on a misunderstanding, for the man, waving the people down with his hand, went on — “I will, however, do so today by way of exception. But such a delay must not be repeated. And now step forward!” Somebody jumped down from the platform, so that a place was cleared for K., onto which he climbed. He stood pressed close against the table; the crush behind him was so great that he had to resist it if he did not want to push the examining magistrate’s table, and perhaps the magistrate himself as well, down off the platform.
